newsitem.title: FRANCE: Volvo says C70 will bring good profit.
newsitem.headline: Volvo says C70 will bring good profit.

text.p: Volvo Cars new C70 coupe and the the coming convertible version will earn a good profit, Volvo Cars CEO Tuve Johannesson told Reuters in an interview on Monday.

"In the C70, we build on the initial investment in the 850 model. What will be brought in on the margin is of big importance. With production at our Uddevalla plant of 20,000 cars a year, we will be way above break-even," he said.
The Uddevalla operation, in cooperation with Britain's TWR, will unveil a convertible in the late autumn of 1997.
For both models, the plant now has a combined capacity of 20,000 cars a year.
"That number can be raised to 30,000 and to 40,000, but that is the absolute maximum for this plant to stay specialized," Johannesson said.
He added that it is hard to say which will be the bigger selling model -- the coupe or the convertible.
"We have chosen to bring out the coupe model first and let it pave the way for the convertible later. Maybe it was not originally planned this way," Johannesson said.
Volvo Cars has no plans to expand into a more expensive segment than the C70, which in Sweden will cost at least $65,000.
"We are now at our uppermost level. We find it better to raise the number of variants in the middle segment," Johannesson said.
He reiterated Volvo Cars new strategy of carefully expanding into new areas and added that the S40/V40 is not an isolated model built on a new platform.

"It resembles the start-up of the 850 model, which we now produce in many variants. But I also want to underline that, so far, we have not talked about a new model built on the S40/V40-platform," Johannesson said.
The S40/V40 is also a good example of what can be achieved cooperating with another company.

"Without the cooperation with Mitsubishi, it would not have been possible to bring forward the S40/V40," he said. Johannesson praised the ability of the Volvo Cars organisation to work with "heavy" external partners like Mitsubishi and TWR and he was certain it would be able to undertake even more cooperation.

"If you ask me a philosophical question, yes we can handle cooperation with more heavy external partners. It is not something that is on line, but theoretically it would not give us problems," Johannesson added.
